title: How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income
description: How to build an emergency fund on a low income: start with $500, where to keep it, how to find $10 to $25 a week, and what to do when you must use it.

cover.alt: A jar of coins kept dry under a colourful umbrella

keywords: emergency fund low income how much emergency fund starter emergency fund save money small income
takeaways: Aim for a starter fund of $500 before you think about three to six months of expenses.
Keep it in a separate account you can reach within a day but don't see every time you pay for something.
$10 a week reaches $500 in 50 weeks. $25 a week gets there in 20.
body:
"Save three to six months of expenses" is the standard advice. On a low income it can sound like "first, become a different person".

You are not alone if a surprise bill would knock you over. In the Federal Reserve's latest household survey, 63% of US adults said they would cover an unexpected $400 expense with cash or its equivalent. That leaves more than a third who would have to borrow, sell something or go without.

So start smaller. A few hundred dollars set aside changes more than you'd expect, because most emergencies aren't disasters. They are a cracked phone screen, a bike repair, a short week at work.

## What an emergency fund is for

It is money whose only job is to stop a surprise from turning into debt.

It **is** for: urgent repairs, medical costs, a gap between jobs, an unplanned trip for family reasons.

It is **not** for: sales, holidays, gifts, or yearly bills you knew were coming. Those are irregular costs and belong in your normal budget.

## How much emergency fund do you need first?

Forget the six-month figure for now. A starter fund of about $500, or one month of your rent share if that is easier to picture, covers a large share of the surprises that push people onto credit cards or into borrowing from friends.

Once you get there, the next levels are:

1. One month of essential expenses
2. Three months of essential expenses
3. Six months, if your income is irregular or other people depend on you

Each level is worth having on its own. You don't need the last one for the first to help.

## Where to keep your emergency fund

Three rules:

- **Separate** from the account you spend from, so the balance isn't looking at you at the checkout.
- **Reachable within a day or so**, with no penalty. This is not money to invest or lock away.
- **No monthly fee.** A basic savings account with no minimum balance is enough. If it pays interest, good, but access matters more than the rate at this stage.

No bank account? A second mobile wallet, or a sealed envelope kept somewhere inconvenient, does the same job. The separation is the point.

## How to find the money on a low income

### Start with an amount that feels too small

Repetition matters more than the amount.

| Weekly amount | Time to reach $500 | After one year |
|---:|---|---:|
| $5 | 100 weeks | $260 |
| $10 | 50 weeks | $520 |
| $15 | About 34 weeks | $780 |
| $25 | 20 weeks | $1,300 |

### Pay the fund first

Move the money on the day you are paid, before anything else. If your bank lets you schedule a transfer, set it once and stop thinking about it. Saving "whatever is left at the end of the month" rarely works, because there is rarely anything left.

### Send it every windfall

Tax refunds, birthday money, a bonus, a refund you had forgotten about. Putting even half of each into the fund can cut months off the timeline.

### Redirect one cost

Pick a single expense to trim and move exactly that amount into the fund the same day. Groceries are a good place to look; here are [25 ways to lower the grocery bill](/blog/save-money-on-groceries-without-coupons/). The transfer is what counts. Money you merely didn't spend gets absorbed somewhere else.

### Earn it separately

Some people find it easier to earn the fund than to cut for it. A few weekends of [side work](/blog/side-hustles-for-students-zero-investment/), with all of it going straight to savings, can build the starter fund in a month or two.

## A realistic example

Here is a made-up but ordinary case. Priya earns about $900 a month from a shop job. She opens a second, free savings account and sets a $10 transfer for every Friday, which is payday.

In March she gets a $120 tax refund and sends half of it, $60, to the fund. In June she sells her old textbooks for $45 and adds that too. By week 40 she has $400 from the weekly transfers and $105 from the extras: $505 in total, ten weeks ahead of schedule.

Nothing dramatic happened. She never saved more than $10 from a normal week. The fund grew because the transfer was automatic and the extras had somewhere to go.

## Emergency fund or debt first?

If you have high-interest debt, do both in this order:

1. Keep paying every minimum.
2. Build the $500 starter fund.
3. Put your extra money toward the debt, using [the snowball or avalanche method](/blog/debt-snowball-vs-avalanche/).
4. Grow the fund to three months once the expensive debt is gone.

Skipping step 2 is tempting because the interest feels urgent. But with no cushion, the first surprise goes straight back on the card.

## When you have to use it

Use it. That is what it's for, and spending it on a real emergency means the plan worked.

Afterwards, restart the same weekly transfer until it is back at the target. Don't raise the amount to "catch up" if that would break your budget.

## Common mistakes

- **Waiting until you can save a "proper" amount.** $5 a week is $260 in a year. That is a proper amount.
- **Keeping it in your everyday account.** It will quietly get spent.
- **Investing it.** Investments can be down at exactly the moment you need the cash.
- **Calling everything an emergency.** If you saw it coming, it belongs in the budget. A [simple monthly budget](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) with a line for irregular costs protects the fund.

## Common questions

**Is $500 really enough?** Not for everything. It is enough to stop the most common small shocks from becoming debt, and it proves to you that you can save.

**Should I use a credit card as my emergency fund?** A card is a backup. At rates above 20%, a $400 repair gets more expensive every month you carry it.

**What if I can't spare anything some weeks?** Skip that week and restart the next. A missed transfer doesn't cancel the habit.

Open the separate account this week and move the first amount, however small. The habit of moving it is what you are building. The balance follows.
